added.name: Orikata Bio PBC
added.long_description:
A new agent, tool, or generative model alone doesn’t solve the whole problem for most research questions. Someone still has to assemble the data, work out which methods to use and get the tools and datasets working together. We’re building Noto, a multiplayer discovery workbench for human and agentic scientists, to bring everyone's favorite frontier models, agents, tools, and scientific models into one shared workspace, so that you can focus on making your next discovery, rather than wrestling with your Python environment or finding GPUs.

Plan an experiment, work with its generated data, run an analysis or model, maybe even train a new model, and keep the results in the notebook. We designed Noto so that the inputs, code, methods and results stay connected across local and hosted compute. Both people and agents need to see how a result was produced and build on it. Biology is where we’re starting, with the workbench being built for more general research across many scientific disciplines.

Available now: our first biological analysis tools, hosted model inference, and an initial agent interface. Free usage is available within limits, alongside paid model runs and individual and team plans. Researchers can run sequence and structure analyses and hosted scientific models without provisioning GPUs or maintaining each model’s dependencies.

In development: the full multiplayer notebook and wider agent workflows and integrations.

Orikata Bio Public Benefit Corporation, or Orikata Bio PBC, is the company. We work under two brands: Orikata Bio for biological discovery and Megure Labs for scientific software.

Biological discovery with Orikata Bio

We’re developing Ibuki, a world-model family for biology, to learn how evolution, sequence, structure and function relate and use those relationships to understand and engineer living systems. We’re pretraining our own protein language models, and developing coordinate and multimodal models for prediction, inverse folding, alignment and generative design. Proteins are our starting point; DNA, RNA, small molecules, and other biological modalities are part of the longer-term direction.

Along the way, we assembled Umi, with over 100 billion unique protein sequences, and Sora, with nearly two billion protein structure records. Having that much data only helps if we can organize it, compare it and find the biology relevant to a particular question. We’re building the full-corpus embedding, indexing and customer access that will bring more of those collections into research workflows.

Our key insight was that the fixed substitution tables used to compare biological sequences are the simplest example of a neural network. Replacing them with contextual substitution operators lets us learn how positions correspond, from reference alignments and directly from molecular geometry. Hikoboshi (open source) turns those learned relationships into tools for sequence and structure alignment, search, clustering and many other evolutionary analysis pipelines.
GitHub: https://github.com/orikata-bio/hikoboshi

Scientific software with Megure Labs

Learning those relationships meant making the alignment calculation itself trainable. Orihime (open source), our differentiable-alignment and structured-attention library, lets neural networks learn through scientific algorithms on CPUs and GPUs. It supplies the training machinery behind our learned alignment methods.
GitHub: https://github.com/megure-labs/orihime

Running the models efficiently is its own problem. Hataya (private evaluation), our inference engine and compiler for scientific models, turns trained models and their dependencies into standalone CPU and GPU programs, carrying the exact weights, identity and verification evidence with them. We’re building it to make both our models and public scientific models cheaper to run, including through Noto’s hosted service.

Kaname coordinates long-running agent work across every model provider: tasks, compute, permissions, retries and the record of what happened. We’re bringing that coordination and provenance into Noto’s research workflows so work can continue across people, agents and machines.

Researchers can start with a single analysis or hosted model run today. Noto is where we’re bringing them together so an analysis or model run can become part of a continuing research project, with the data, methods and results kept alongside it.

Try Noto’s live tools: https://megure.ai/noto/workspace/
Biological tools: https://orikata.ai/tools/
Scientific software: https://megure.ai/
Biological discovery: https://orikata.ai/
Open source: https://github.com/megure-labs and https://github.com/orikata-bio
For research use, questions about the data or private evaluations: casey@orikata.ai
added.one_liner: A multiplayer discovery workspace for human and agentic scientists

Bento sits directly in the production loop and gives teams the operational leverage required to scale agent ecosystems without scaling human firefighting alongside them. The result is a system that turns opaque agents into agents that can be monitored, debugged, and improved continuously.

The founders learned this problem at Emergent (YC S24), where they built and operated production coding agents used by 5M+ users. Abhinav was hire #1 and helped Emergent hit SWE-Bench #1 and scale from $0 to $100M ARR in just 8 months. Kaushik was hire #2, led full-stack engineering at Emergent, and was key to building the infrastructure that made production agents reliable, observable, and debuggable. long_description.before:
Coding agents now write more code than teams can check, making verification pipelines the new bottleneck. Graphide builds that verification, starting with CI.

Graphide CI runs faster and cheaper because we own both the hardware and the optimizations and configs that run on it, which lets us do what owning only one could not. A graph of the codebase runs only the tests each change can reach, and always-on agents tune machines, caches and test splits together, around the clock. Optionally, we also patch the tests themselves with our own libraries so they run faster. We have seen most of our customers cut CI time 80-95% compared to their existing setups.

Our PR review agent then runs the old and new code in our live environments, finding bugs and proving them by writing tests, as well as analyzing synthetic and production data through the PR before it merges.

Finally, our visualizer allows you to see these data flows and graph based diffs to both easily analyze the found bugs, run custom data flows, and see / understand a PR in seconds.

Graphide's focus is on verifying the code agents write.
long_description.after:
Graphide CI runs your CI 10-20× faster than GitHub runners, and our 24/7 agents optimize the CI itself, not just the machines. For teams with big CI bills that haven't been optimized, we cut costs 70%+ and take over the ongoing work of optimizing CI, so you can focus on your product.

We're faster and cheaper because we own both the hardware and the optimizations and configs that run on it, which lets us do what owning only one could not. Our agents then tune machines, caches and test splits as you add more tests and code over time. long_description.before:
Acyclic builds the infrastructure for agent swarms: open-source primitives for running agents in parallel, and a managed agents platform that runs swarms for you. Complex, long-running tasks are split across many agents, each working in its own instant fork of the workspace, and finish in a fraction of the time.

We built Acyclic because we believe there are huge gains to be had in how agents are run, beyond the models themselves. Agents can already do real work, but they still do it one step at a time, so complex tasks take hours or days. Running them as swarms is an infrastructure problem: isolating each agent, dividing the work, and merging the results without conflicts. Today, teams use Acyclic to run heavy document-processing pipelines in minutes instead of hours.

At Cambridge, we researched ML and auto-parallelising compilers, and then we built multi-agent systems in production: Ram as a Palantir FDE for pharma clients, shipping systems for clinical trial design, and Varun leading agent architecture at Tracelight for Big 4 accounting firms. We kept asking the same question: the agents were good enough, so why couldn't we run thousands of them at once to make everything faster and cheaper? Acyclic is our answer.
long_description.after:
We’re building the foundations of agent swarms that can materially accelerate all work: benchmarks to measure model capabilities, models trained to coordinate thousands of agents, RL environments to improve them, and infrastructure that can put a datacenter’s worth of compute behind a single conversation within seconds.

Both founders graduated top 10% from Cambridge. Ram is a published ML researcher and Varun worked at the frontier of parallel programming languages and shipped enterprise multi-agent systems at Palantir and Tracelight. We realised that agents were good enough to solve most use cases. So why couldn’t we run thousands of them at once and finish hours of work in minutes?

one_liner.before: Agent swarms that make long-running tasks exponentially faster
one_liner.after: Benchmarks, RL envs and infra for scaling agent swarms

More than 65 enterprise marketing teams, including Envoy, Eclypsium, Cover Genius, Fortinet, CoStar, Bagel Brands, and Family Express, use Gather to continually fight AI slop and create original on-brand, third-party validated thought leadership, reports, ebooks, and campaign content.

The value of that research compounds. Every interview adds to a foundation of quantitative, qualitative, and voice data from over 300,000 real interviews across customers, with thousands added monthly. Our models use that understanding to predict how buyers will respond to messaging, pricing, and market shifts. Each answer includes supporting evidence and a confidence level. When confidence is low, Gather automatically runs new research.
